definition: A debugger stopping point associated with an execution location and optionally a condition. Stopping changes the timing of the running system.
A debugger check that can stop when a watched expression changes, or for supported read/access conditions. Hardware support and software overhead depend on the target and debugger.
The GNU debugger, a tool for inspecting and controlling program execution. Debugging a microcontroller requires suitable target and probe support as well as the program image.
Hardware connecting a computer's debugging tools to a target's supported debug interface. The device, wiring and voltage requirements must match the target.
Extra observations added to a program, such as bounded event logging. Their timing and storage costs can change the behaviour being measured.
A test executed on the development computer rather than the target board. It can validate exercised logic cases without testing the real peripheral interface or target timing.
A deliberately controlled replacement for a dependency, used here to supply known device outcomes to application tests. A fake's behaviour must match the particular contract a test relies on.
A program check expressing an expected condition. In the C tests here, a failing assert reports failure and terminates execution when assertions are enabled.
A C preprocessor macro that disables the standard assert checks when defined at the relevant header inclusion. Leave it undefined in these assertion-based test builds.
A specific input or event sequence paired with an expected result. Boundary and failure cases complement ordinary successful examples.
A test at or just around a specified limit, such as values immediately below and at an alert threshold. It helps distinguish neighbouring interpretations of the rule.

A device or mechanism that requests a configured recovery action if software stops supplying the required refreshes. Its useful meaning depends on what progress those refreshes are intended to demonstrate.
An operation that restarts or reloads a watchdog's waiting interval. Refreshing blindly can conceal a stalled application, so the application must define the required current progress evidence.

The application's explicit rule for which recent progress observations justify continued operation or a watchdog refresh. Correctly handled device failures may be allowed under a documented degraded-operation policy.
The interval for which the application evaluates current health evidence. A progress flag from an earlier interval must not silently stand in for new progress.
Device-provided information about why execution restarted, interpreted according to that device's reset and boot documentation. Read useful evidence before actions that clear or replace it.
A deliberately specified mode that remains responsive while some capability is unavailable. It must report its limits rather than present missing data as a successful measurement.
An application policy that keeps a fault state active until a specified recovery action occurs. A later ordinary input does not automatically erase the recorded fault.

An explicit application input that begins a chosen recovery transition. In the example model, RESET clears the fault state back to waiting for fresh data; it does not itself operate a physical reset circuit.
An operating system providing mechanisms for organising tasks, scheduling and waiting under timing requirements. Using one does not by itself prove that every application deadline will be met.
A scheduled execution context with state and stack storage. A single core executes one task at an instant, while other tasks may be ready or waiting.
A task that is eligible to be selected for execution under the kernel's scheduling rules. It differs from a task blocked while waiting for an event.
A task waiting for a supported event or time condition rather than being eligible for immediate execution. Other eligible work may use the processor while it waits.
A scheduling action that replaces currently executing work with another eligible execution context. Exact trigger and priority rules depend on the kernel, configuration and interrupt state.
A scheduling rank used to select among ready tasks under a kernel's rules. Priority does not remove execution-time limits or waiting for shared resources.

A scheduling arrangement that allows eligible work to take turns using a processor. Equal-priority time sharing is a configuration-dependent feature in the RTOS example, not an assumption for every kernel.
The amount of stack storage reserved and checked for an execution context. Each task's stack must support its actual call and interrupt-related usage under the target's rules.

Memory reserved for an RTOS task's active function calls and saved execution information under its target port's rules. Each task needs enough storage for its actual call depth and local data; a separate task does not share one unlimited stack with all other tasks.
A rule assigning responsibility for a shared peripheral or protecting access to it. Scheduling tasks does not automatically make simultaneous driver calls correct.
A finite communication mechanism through which tasks can exchange items under a kernel's API contract. The application must decide how to handle a full queue or a timed-out wait.
A C type describing named integer alternatives using enum. Named states make the project's decision cases easier to identify than unexplained numeric labels.
The C expression using condition, question mark and colon to select between two result expressions. Only the selected result expression is evaluated.
The application boundary translating a particular driver's inputs and outcomes into the logic model's events and outputs. It needs checking on the actual target separately from the pure host model.
The one final result assigned to an acquisition attempt, such as a decoded sample or a timeout. Ending an attempt once prevents a stale second outcome from being dispatched for the same work.
An identified version of the program source. Recording it with build settings helps make an observed result reproducible.
A previously checked firmware image kept as part of a supported recovery workflow. It is useful evidence from known conditions, not a guarantee for every later hardware configuration.
